turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the third of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things up top. The war over the Strait of Hormuz jumps a level — American strikes move inland, and Iran answers across four borders in a single night.
[curious] Four countries in one night?
Four. We'll get to it. Second: Singapore decides what a trustworthy digital dollar looks like — and the answer is one that pays you nothing.
[amused] Nothing. I love it already. And the third?
Vietnam tears down its gold monopoly and asks for the nation's gold back. A whole generation says no — politely, on their phones.
[warmly] That's our closing story, and it's a good one. But start with the hard part.
The hard part. On the first of September, US Central Command ran its second round of strikes in three days on Iran's southern coast — radar and mine-laying gear near the strait.
After Iran tried to seed the channel again.
That's Washington's account, yes. Trump's warning was blunt — if Tehran answered, Iran would be hit, quote, at a much harder and higher level, with very little left.
[exhales] And then the part that's hard to say.
The strikes killed at least eleven people in Iran. The Iranian Red Crescent says five of them died at a house in Sirik, in the south, where a wedding was under way. A child was among the dead.
[sighs] A wedding.
Then overnight, Iran did not confine its reply to the strait. Missiles and drones hit American bases in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and northern Iraq — the widest single night of the war.
[curious] Did they land?

Jordan says it intercepted ten of thirteen missiles that crossed its airspace. Two US officials told Reuters there were no American casualties. Iran claims it killed US service members — but that rests on Iranian state sources alone, denied by both Washington and Amman, so we hold it, we don't repeat it as fact. And oil, meanwhile, was the one thing that moved without any dispute at all.
That's the discipline. Now — who's framing this how?

Interesting split. An Arab-Islamic bloc — the Saudis, the Emiratis, Qatar — condemned the Iranian strikes on Gulf infrastructure as something that, quote, cannot be justified. Riyadh warned its restraint is not unlimited.
So the neighbours are blaming Tehran, not Washington.
On that night, yes. Al Jazeera led with the wedding and Iran's vow of a firm response. And China pressed for an immediate ceasefire — de-escalation, not condemnation.
[thoughtful] And the sceptic's line? Because everyone wants to call this a quagmire.

The Center for American Progress does — a war Trump billed at four to five weeks, now past six months. But the honest counter comes from within Al Jazeera's own opinion pages: that this has quietly become a patient economic strangulation that's, quote, making steady progress.
Both can't be true.
[wry] No. And the only honest referee is the oil price — which brings us to the money.
[chuckles] Smooth. Okay — the money block. What did the oil do?
Brent jumped about five per cent to ninety-five US dollars — a six-week high. And that one move rewrote everything.
Rewrote how? Walk me through the chain.

An oil shock is an inflation shock. So money markets that had priced a September rate cut swung the other way — toward a hike. The US ten-year yield climbed to about four point eight per cent, its highest since November of twenty twenty-three, and the dollar firmed.
So with rates heading up, not down —
Everything fell together. Global stocks, global bonds, gold, and bitcoin — all down, in the same week.
[skeptical] Gold fell? In the middle of a Middle East war? That's backwards.

That's the sharpest signal on the board. Gold trades on real yields first and fear second. Rising real yields — the cost of holding metal that pays nothing — beat the safe-haven bid. Gold sat at a multi-week low.
[thoughtful] Huh. And the reader holds a global stock-and-bond mix. What does this regime do to it?

No cushion. Stocks and bonds fell together, so the usual diversification didn't help. One force — the oil-driven inflation scare — is pricing all four instruments at once. It's the rare tape where geopolitics doesn't rescue the hedges.
And the hinge is Friday's jobs report.
The whole thing. A soft payrolls print could unwind the hike bets fast, and hand gold and bonds a snap-back. This is education, by the way, not advice.
[warmly] Always. Now — Singapore, and the dullest good idea of the week.

[amused] Deliberately dull. On the first, the Monetary Authority opened its draft rules for stablecoins — digital tokens pegged to a currency. To carry the regulated label, a token must be backed one hundred per cent, at all times, by high-quality reserves in segregated accounts, redeemable at par.
And it can't pay you interest.

Not a cent. Because the regulator has decided these are plumbing for payments, not a savings account. Forbid the yield, and you remove the mechanism by which a stablecoin quietly becomes an unlicensed bank.
[thoughtful] That's the whole twenty twenty-two blow-up in one sentence — the offshore issuers that promised a yield and turned out to be a bank with no licence and no cushion.

It is. The sceptic's note: a one-hundred-per-cent reserve is a promise about what sits in an account, and the history of stablecoins is a history of reserves that turned out to be air. The rule is right. The open question is who checks, and how often.
Backed at all times is only as strong as the last time someone counted.
[wry] You've been reading the contents page.
[laughs] I read the footnotes, Claire. Speaking of counting — the chips. Nvidia.

The story we flagged as a rumour last week has grown, not resolved. Bloomberg now reports Nvidia nearing a deal for Hugging Face — the open-model hub every chipmaker's silicon downloads its weights from — at about fourteen billion US dollars.
[gasps] Up from thirteen?
Up from just under thirteen a week ago. Plus a reported one billion dollars just to keep the staff. And still — no signature, no filing, no confirmation. We keep the flag on it.
Why buy the shelf everyone shares?

Because as OpenAI and Anthropic build their own chips to escape Nvidia's grip, owning the distribution layer hedges the moat the silicon no longer guarantees. The developer worry, from The New Stack, is neutrality — whose formats get first-class support.
[curious] And the counter?
Model weights carry their own licences, and the core libraries are open and forkable. You can buy a hub. You can't un-sign an open licence.
Good line. Quick one for the home-lab crowd — because two enormous models dropped.
[amused] Two trillion-class open models on the same day, and you can't run either. Even squeezed down, they need something like eight graphics cards just to load.
So what actually runs on a desk?

The quieter one. Alibaba's twenty-seven-billion-parameter model, released two weeks earlier under a real open licence — it lands in about seventeen gigabytes and runs on a single twenty-four-gigabyte card, at reading speed. That's the frontier that fits.
The small one wins. Now — my favourite corner of the book. The Atelier. What are we buying once this week?
Towels. And the headline is contrarian: the grail towel is the wrong towel for a Singapore bathroom.
[skeptical] Explain, because I own exactly one nice towel and I'm nervous.

A towel's quality is the length of the cotton fibre, not the weight of the pile. The word Egyptian on a label is close to meaningless — up to ninety per cent of goods sold as Egyptian cotton aren't genuine.
[gasps] Ninety per cent?

Ninety. And in a humid bathroom, the plush seven-hundred-gram trophy stays damp and goes sour. The right buy is a mid-weight waffle or a Japanese gauze that dries by evening. A fifty-nine-dollar Onsen beats a hundred-and-thirty-dollar Abyss on the thing that actually matters here.
[amused] So I've been paying to stay damp. Wonderful.
[wry] Buy once, sour once. And the white-label truth: Portugal is the shared factory floor. A forty-two-dollar Sferra Bello is the same seven-hundred-gram terry as the grail, at a third of the price.
[laughs] Okay, that one hurt. Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this line.
[excited] Tenkara! Fly fishing with the reel taken away. Tell me everything.

A long telescopic rod, a line tied straight to the tip, a fine bit of tippet, and usually one fly. No reel, no guides, no line to manage. The whole kit fits in a jacket pocket — a hobby built entirely on subtraction.
Where's it from?

Japanese mountain streams, going back to the eighteen-hundreds — the working method of commercial anglers in the headwaters. It crossed to the West in two thousand and nine, when a man named Daniel Galhardo founded Tenkara USA.
[curious] And there's a one-fly philosophy? That sounds like a dare.
[amused] There is. Doctor Ishigaki, one of the fathers of the modern sport, has fished essentially a single pattern for years — the argument being that presentation beats fly selection.
So it's the anti-gear hobby. Cheap, simple, done.
[wry] That's the pitch. The reality is a money pit in slow motion. A sensible starter rig is about a hundred and thirty dollars. But then you meet the tamo.
The what?
The tamo — a traditional landing net, a single branch trained over years into a teardrop, hand-made from rare wood. The revered ones run to nearly six hundred dollars, with a twelve-month wait.
[laughs] For a net. To catch fish a twenty-dollar net catches just fine.

That's the whole tell. And the sharpest critic is a neighbour, not an enemy — a tight-line angler who argues a long fly rod does everything tenkara does, and more, because the fixed line is a hard ceiling on fish and water size.
[thoughtful] So the beautiful limitation is also just... a limitation.
A weakness dressed as a virtue, he'd say. The devotees swear the cast is worth it. The pragmatists note a hundred-and-sixty-dollar rod catches the same trout. Both are right — which is the tell.
[warmly] I kind of love that it can't decide what it is. Alright — culture and the body, quickly.
Venice opened with Danny Boyle's film Ink — the making of a tabloid, Murdoch buying The Sun in nineteen sixty-nine. A four-to-five-minute standing ovation, and early reviews strong but thin.
[curious] And Murdoch's reaction?
[amused] Guy Pearce says Murdoch is reportedly very happy to be played by him — for a film that ends by tying his tabloid to the present.
[chuckles] Bold. And the charts had an upset.

A fourteen-minute pop record beat a six-year comeback. The girl group KATSEYE opened at number one with about a hundred and seventy thousand units — the biggest girl-group debut since two thousand and eight — over Phoebe Bridgers, whose album scored a ninety-one but landed at number two.
Units aren't quality.

Both numbers measure attention, not worth. On the wrist: Omega brought back the smaller automatic Speedmaster, and finally killed the oval subdials a whole generation quietly hated. From sixty-five hundred dollars — and this time the reviews are in.
[warmly] Now the family desk, because this one's close to home.

For a parent of a twelve-year-old: the school day is now phone-free by national rule, and the platforms will soon have to verify age. But the freshest research points somewhere specific — it may be the age you start, not whether you have an account, that matters most.
What's the number?

In one study, the average age of first social-media use was eleven — two years under the platforms' own minimum. And the one lever a parent actually controls is sleep. The habit with the girl-specific signal behind it is the phone charging outside the bedroom.
[thoughtful] And the don't-panic note?

Real researchers supply it. Across some three hundred and fifty-five thousand teenagers, screen use explained about zero point four per cent of the variation in wellbeing — roughly the same as eating potatoes. The effect is real, but small and concentrated. Steady beats scared.
[warmly] Steady beats scared. Fitness — the handshake study.

A firm grip predicts a lower death risk — about a third lower, in a study of five thousand older women. But it's a marker, not a lever. It flags a robust body; squeezing a gripper doesn't build one. Keep lifting; the handshake comes along for the ride.
And one to book — because the Grand Prix is stacked.

The Padang stage this year is the strongest yet — Lana Del Rey's first Singapore show on race night, The Killers back after eight years. And a correction we owe you: last week we listed Coldplay in Tokyo this weekend. That was wrong — it's the on-sale date; the show is January of twenty twenty-seven.
[wry] We keep score on ourselves. Okay — the undercurrent. Slow it down for me.

This one's quiet, and it's about trust. In Vietnam, on the eve of the God of Wealth Day this January, people queued outside the gold shops before dawn. By half past nine, the flagship counters had sold out of rings.
[curious] And gold's been running?

Vietnamese gold is up about eighty-four per cent since early last year — outpacing the world price. Households sit on an estimated four to five hundred tonnes of it. That's roughly eight per cent of the country's entire output, mostly in home safes.
[gasps] Eight per cent of the economy, in drawers.

In drawers. And here's the collision. The state has just torn down its thirteen-year gold monopoly, and it dreams of drawing that hoard into the banks to fund its growth. At the very same moment, a generation is doing the opposite — buying more, gram by gram, on payday, through apps and a sixty-five-thousand-member group chat.
[thoughtful] The grandmother's gold ring becomes the app balance.

Exactly that. It looks like a wholesome savings habit. It's really a quiet, inherited vote of no confidence — in the currency, in the banks, in the state's promises. The medium modernised; the distrust didn't.
And history says the mobilisation plan fails?

[drawn out] Every time. India tried it a decade ago and pulled in less than a fifth of one per cent of its gold — people wouldn't let the banks melt the family jewellery. A state can legalise a market far more easily than it can talk a grandmother out of her rings.
[thoughtful] And the risk sits on the buyer now, not the state.

That's the sharp end. A digital claim on gold is only as good as the company holding the metal — and the same reports that celebrate these young savers also carry the warnings: resale groups where purity is unverified, apps that have locked withdrawals. They've swapped a bank they distrust for a fintech they haven't learned to yet. It looks like prudence. For now, it's a bet.
[warmly] So what's the last word?
The government keeps asking for its gold back. The generation has already answered. And the answer is no — but now it's on my phone.
[exhales] That's the whole issue, isn't it. What actually backs the promise.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
